children: By Beckie Strum
America's wealthiest house hunters aren't shying away from higher mortgage rates. In fact, demand for multimillion-dollar loans is booming.

Heightened mortgage rates have dashed dreams of homeownership for many Americans, sidelined wishful buyers, and dragged U.S. home sales to record lows. Yet the spike in so-called superjumbo loans defies the prevailing narrative that the ultrarich are paying cash to avoid high mortgage rates, which are now barreling back toward 8%.
"We are seeing sizable growth in the share of loans that are being taken out above $5 million," said Joel Berner, a senior economist at Realtor.com.

Originations over $5 million spiked more than 50% last year compared with 2024, according to Home Mortgage Disclosure Act, or HMDA, data provided by the Mortgage Bankers Association, which provided the most recently available data. Loans at that price level totaled $17.8 billion in 2025, an annual increase of about 53%, the data show.

No doubt last year was a better year for borrowers. Average mortgage rates dipped into the low-6% range in the second half of 2025. But the rebound was far more subdued for average folks than for the ultrawealthy. Overall mortgage originations rose only about 10% in 2025 year over year, according to the HMDA data.

Affluent home buyers have more financial flexibility to navigate the ups and downs of mortgage rates by paying cash or turning to alternative lending products, such as borrowing against their appreciated stock portfolios. As a result, the luxury segment has proved a bright spot in an otherwise beleaguered housing market.

But the ultrawealthy aren't simply dipping into cash. For instance, $1 million-plus loans made up 3.4% of all U.S. mortgages in 2025, compared with just 1.6% in 2020, according to data provided by Realtor.com.
Need examples? Take the case of Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel.

The pharma exec and his wife, Brenda, sold their town house in Boston's historic Beacon Hill neighborhood for $10.4 million in November to a local buyer who paid for it with a whopping $6.24 million home loan courtesy of Rocket Mortgage, according to public property records. The Massachusetts-based buyer didn't respond to a request for comment.

Ultrarich home buyers more commonly go through their private banks, which have seen demand for multimillion-dollar loans rise noticeably since last year, even as rates remain stubbornly high. As of Monday, the average 30-year jumbo rate was 7.44%, even higher than the conventional 30-year mortgage rate by a few basis points, according to figures from Bankrate.com.

"It's a little bit unexpected," said Jon Kessler, executive vice president and head of credit and cash management solutions at PNC Private Bank. "We had a view that maybe this activity would fall off a little bit due to the rising rate environment, but it has been fairly consistent and fairly strong."

A booming stock market explains some of the motivation to take out superjumbo mortgages. The S&P 500 is up 12% this year alone. Investors figure that's a much better return than tying up cash in a mansion that sees marginal annual appreciation, if any, during a weak housing market.
"They're going to deploy those funds in those opportunities and not use their cash to pay down loans or buy real estate. They'd rather borrow," Kessler said.

It isn't only equities. Wealthy investors have doubled down on alternative assets, which tend to be illiquid, tying up funds in private equity, commercial real estate and directly in their own businesses. TIGER 21, a peer network of ultra-high-net-worth individuals, found in a recent survey that its members' cash reserves are at their lowest level since the organization began tracking in 2007, as the rich shift their wealth into growth sectors.

Recent examples abound of seven- and even eight-figure home loans. In July, an unknown buyer snapped up casino mogul Steve Wynn's Beverly Hills megamansion for $47.75 million with an eye-watering $28.5 million mortgage, according to public records on PropertyShark. UBS Bank financed the loan for the superjumbo house spanning 27,000 square feet, according to public records, which also show this was to be used as a second home.

Likewise, NBA All-Star and Washington Wizard player Anthony Davis sold his Los Angeles mansion — with a 35-foot domed ceiling — in July to Miriam Schaeffer, a former executive at nail polish giant OPI, for $32 million. Schaeffer, who didn't respond to a request for comment, borrowed $20.8 million from JPMorgan Chase to finance the grand, eight-bedroom estate, property records show.

Even independent mortgage lenders, who don't have the deep relationships with wealthy clients that private banks do, are seeing healthy demand for multimillion loans. Such is the case at Prosperity Home Mortgage, a subsidiary of HomeServices of America, a Berkshire Hathaway Affiliate, said Justin Messer, its president and CEO.
"Year over year, the cash-buying percentage has gone down a little. People are financing a little bit more," Messer said. "They don't want to burn through their liquidity."

The rise in multimillion-dollar home loans is another example of the K-shaped economy. The wealthiest house hunters are reaping the rewards of softening prices and more negotiable sellers, while average buyers get "crushed" by mortgage rates, Berner said.
There was an uptick in big-ticket home sales last year, with $5 million-plus transactions increasing 8%, mostly driven by a rise in trophy sales over $10 million, according to Realtor.com data.
Buying conditions are "phenomenal" for people who can pay cash — or shrug off a 7% mortgage rate, Berner said.
"You're really at an advantage right now because there are just so few buyers, and sellers are willing to make a deal. We're seeing a lot of price cuts," he said.
High-flying buyers may be thinking they can refinance in a few years or simply pay off the mortgage early when they see an opportunity to sell stocks or reshuffle assets.
"If you've got that kind of flexibility and there are reasons that you would want to do this right now, I think that does make sense," Berner said.
